sections.content: This section introduces the central theme of the chapter: the enduring relevance and significance of temples in Indian culture. It argues that despite modernization, urbanization, and the passage of time, temples continue to hold a persistent grip on the masses. The text contrasts old, ruined temples with the far more numerous active ones, noting an increase in both new temples and attendance. The author posits that this is because religion has always been the dominant note in Indian culture, with temple worship being its characteristic expression. The rise of this 'temple culture' is attributed primarily to the Āgama literature. The section also touches upon the changing role of temples, which were once integrated local institutions (social, economic, educational) in the medieval period but have become more isolated, especially in urban areas. The distinction is made between public temples (built by collective effort) and household shrines (gṛharcā). It further categorizes temples into two types: large, magnificent, artistically sophisticated temples patronized by the wealthy, and simple, humble, spontaneous roadside shrines. The former's worship is governed by Āgama, while the latter's is more informal. The section concludes by defining formal temples as products of conscious, institutionalized effort, designed to be monumental and often associated with royalty, with the Āgama literature providing the detailed prescriptions for their construction and function.
sections.summary: This section establishes the continued relevance of temples in India, attributing the rise of 'temple culture' to the Āgama literature. It contrasts the integrated role of medieval temples with their modern isolation and distinguishes between magnificent, Āgama-governed formal temples and simple, informal folk shrines.

sections.content: This section traces the historical origins of formal temples in India. It points to the earliest evidence from the second and first centuries B.C., citing the Brāhmī inscriptions at Besnagar (Heliodorus' column for Vāsudeva) and Ghosuṇḍi (stone-enclosure for Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva). While not explicitly temples, these monuments suggest the presence of shrines. The author notes that both donors were Bhāgavata enthusiasts, suggesting the Bhāgavata cult and its emphasis on bhakti (devotion) spurred the creation of public places for congregational worship. However, monumental evidence (rock-cut or structural) is scarce until the fifth century A.D. Inscriptional evidence from the first and second centuries A.D. (Khāravela, Gāthā-saptaśatī) and the fifth century A.D. (Bilsad, Mandasor) confirms the existence of temples. The earliest surviving structural temples, like the brick temple at Bhitargāon and the stone Daśāvatāra temple at Deogarh, are dated to the Gupta period (fifth century). The section argues that cults of Viṣṇu and Śiva provided the initial impetus for formal temples, which were often built upon pre-existing folk-shrines dedicated to the mother-goddess, frequently located in caves (Guheśvarī). The installation of an icon (mūrti) of Viṣṇu or Śiva in these folk-shrines represents the grafting of the formal temple idiom onto the folk tradition. The composition of Āgama texts is placed after the appearance of these early temples, created to define their status and prescribe worship rituals.
sections.summary: This section explores the historical development of early shrines and temples, starting with inscriptional evidence from the 2nd-1st centuries B.C. linked to the Bhāgavata cult. It identifies the Gupta period (5th century A.D.) as the time when the earliest surviving structural temples appeared. The author suggests formal temples of Viṣṇu and Śiva evolved from and were often built upon older folk-shrines dedicated to the mother-goddess, with Āgama texts emerging later to codify their construction and worship.

sections.content: This section details the Āgama literature's role in temple architecture and worship. The Āgamas are described as an elaborate, encyclopedic temple-lore in Sanskrit, broadly grouped into Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and Śākta divisions. The author suggests they were composed mostly after the ninth century A.D. to codify and formalize pre-existing temple construction and worship customs, incorporating regional practices. Temple culture is presented as incidental to image-worship (arcā). The Viṣṇu-saṁhitā is quoted to emphasize the necessity of a form for meditation. God is conceived with two aspects: transcendental (para, nirākāra) and empirical/worship-worthy (apara, sākāra). The temple is metaphorically described as the body (deha) of the godhead, with the icon being its soul (jīva). Temples are classified into five types: svayam-vyakta (self-manifested), daivika (by celestial beings), ārṣa (by sages), paurāṇa (acclaimed in purāṇas), and mānuṣa (built by humans). The section then focuses on the mānuṣa type, detailing building materials (stone, brick, wood), construction types (śuddha, miśra, saṃkīrṇa), and the six-membered ('ṣaḍ-varga') vertical structure typical of South Indian temples: adhiṣ-ṭhāna (basement), pāda (walls/columns), prastāra (entablature), kaṇṭha (neck), śikhara (tower over sanctum), and stūpī (pinnacle). It also describes the horizontal plan, including the garbha-gṛha (sanctum), maṇḍapas (halls) of various functions, the dhvaja-stambha (flag-post), and bali-pīṭha (offering platform). The section concludes with descriptions of the surrounding wall (prākāra) and the gate-tower (gopura), noting that tall gopuras became characteristic of South Indian temples during the Chola, Pāṇḍya and Vijayanagara periods.
sections.summary: This section elaborates on the Āgama texts as the primary source for codifying temple architecture and worship rituals. It discusses the philosophy of image worship, classifies temples into five types, and provides a detailed breakdown of the architectural components of a typical South Indian temple, covering both its vertical ('ṣaḍ-varga') and horizontal layouts, including the sanctum, various halls (maṇḍapas), and the iconic gate-towers (gopuras).

sections.content: This section examines the temple's multifaceted role as a public institution with social, economic, and political dimensions. It highlights the temple as a major employer of priests, artisans, musicians, and suppliers, and as a large consumer of local goods. Affluent temples functioned as centers for mass-feeding, providing free food (prasāda) to devotees, pilgrims, and the poor, which required an elaborate economic organization. They also offered social services like free lodging (choultries/chatra) and venues for social functions like marriages at minimal cost. Many temples were significant centers of learning, functioning as universities (mahā-ghaṭikā-sthāna), especially those managed by the Kālāmukhas in the South. Examples like the Kedāreśvara temple at Balligāme are cited, where Vedas, philosophy, and other subjects were taught. Temples also encouraged arts like music and dance, often having a dedicated dance-hall (Raṅga-maṇḍapa). The text mentions the 'deva-dāsī' system and the employment of musicians like pipers and drummers (nāgasvara-meḷa). Monastic organizations ('maṭhas') were often associated with temples, as seen with the Kālāmukha sect in Karnataka. The section concludes by describing the annual temple festival ('jātra'), a major socio-economic event attracting large crowds for pilgrimage, trade, and entertainment, serving as a source of revenue for both the temple and the local administration.
sections.summary: This section details the temple's diverse functions beyond worship, portraying it as a central institution in community life. It served as an economic hub, an employer, a provider of social services like food and lodging, a center for education and the arts (music, dance), and the focal point for major socio-economic festivals ('jātra').

sections.content: This section focuses on the two distinct functions of a temple: religious and administrative. While worship is the responsibility of priests, the temple's role as a public institution requires a formal administrative structure, a 'non-āgamic preoccupation'. Richly endowed temples, often receiving land grants (deva-bhoga) from royalty, became significant landlords. This necessitated a complex administrative setup to manage lands, collect revenue, prevent misappropriation, and handle legal matters. The temple's wealth also included buildings, gardens, and valuable offerings like jewels and garments, which required a treasury and secure management. The administrative machinery operated within prevailing social and legal frameworks, with kings as the supreme authorities in ancient times. In practice, temples had their own administrative councils ('sabhā') of local dignitaries. The text describes the evolution of temple administration, mentioning roles like 'dharma-darśis' (volunteer administrators) and hereditary 'sthānikas' (heads/managers of the temple, sthāna-pati). The sthānika was the highest authority but was answerable to the ruler or village council. The section provides a detailed case study of temple administration in the erstwhile state of Mysore, tracing the changes from Tippu Sultan's era (1788), through the British period with the establishment of the Muzarai department, to the post-rendition period and the enactment of various regulations and acts (e.g., Mysore Religious and Charitable Institution Act of 1927). This history shows a progressive shift towards governmental control over temple administration.
sections.summary: This section outlines the dual religious and administrative functions of a temple. It explains how endowments made temples wealthy landlords, necessitating a complex, secular administrative structure to manage property, finances, and legal issues. The evolution of this administration is traced from local councils ('sabhā') and hereditary managers ('sthānikas') to increasing government control, exemplified by the history of the Muzarai department in Mysore.

sections.content: This final section describes the various personnel involved in a temple's operation, dividing them into administrative and religious roles. It begins by outlining the administrative functionaries prevalent in major temples, based on the Mysore model: the 'peṣkār' (principal executive officer), 'pārupattegāra' (supervisor of routine activities), 'nagadi-gumāsta' (accountant), 'jinasi-gumāsta' (in charge of provisions and the storeroom), and 'manegāra' (in charge of services). The text then shifts to the religious functionaries, whose primary purpose is public worship (parārtha). It notes that priesthood was often a hereditary, professional calling. In the temple's administrative hierarchy, priests occupy a secondary position but are central to its religious life. The chief priest ('sannidhi-arcaka' or 'melu-śānti') has the exclusive privilege of entering the sanctum and touching the deity. He is assisted by others like the 'sannidhi-paricāraka' or 'kīḷu-śānti'. Other priests ('devakaris') perform duties outside the sanctum, such as cleaning, bringing water, preparing sandal-paste, and offering 'bali'. The section also lists specialized roles like priests for fire-sacrifices, cooks, reciters of Veda and hymns, the temple astrologer ('purohita'), and musicians. Finally, it mentions a third class of non-religious, non-administrative functionaries, including guards, palanquin bearers, torch-bearers, cleaners, suppliers of flowers, and musicians playing various instruments. Some temples also have a 'tantri', an Āgama expert who supervises all worship rituals.
sections.summary: This section provides a comprehensive list of temple personnel, categorizing them into administrative, religious, and support staff. It details the hierarchy and specific duties of administrative officers (peṣkār, pārupattegāra, etc.) and the various priests, from the chief priest ('sannidhi-arcaka') with exclusive access to the sanctum to those performing ancillary rituals. It also covers numerous support functionaries essential for the temple's daily operations.

chapter_summary: Chapter III, 'Temple Culture,' provides a comprehensive analysis of the Hindu temple as a central institution in Indian life. It argues that temple culture, formalized by the Āgama literature, has shown remarkable persistence despite societal changes. The chapter traces the historical evolution of temples from early folk shrines to monumental, royally-patronized structures. It offers a detailed breakdown of temple architecture, both vertical and horizontal, as prescribed by the Āgamas. Beyond its religious core, the temple is examined as a multifaceted institution with significant social, economic, educational, and artistic functions. The text delves into the complexities of temple administration, charting its development from local community management to extensive governmental control. Finally, it presents a detailed taxonomy of the various functionaries—administrative, priestly, and auxiliary—that constitute the living ecosystem of a temple, highlighting the intricate division of labor required for its operation.
key_arguments: Temples are not mere historical survivals but remain deeply relevant in contemporary Indian society.
The Āgama literature was the major factor that formalized and institutionalized 'temple culture,' codifying architecture, iconography, and worship rituals.
Formal, monumental temples often evolved from or incorporated earlier, simpler folk shrines, particularly those dedicated to the mother-goddess.
The temple's function extends far beyond the religious sphere, acting as a pivotal hub for economic activity, social services, education, and the arts.

Temple administration is a distinct, largely secular function that grew in complexity with the temple's wealth and societal importance, leading to an ongoing tension and eventual shift from local control to government oversight.
key_takeaways: The persistence of temple culture is a key feature of Indian society.
The Āgamas are the foundational texts for understanding the principles behind formal temple construction and worship.
There is a fundamental distinction between magnificent, Āgama-governed temples and simple, spontaneous folk shrines.
Historically, temples were deeply integrated into all aspects of community life: social, economic, educational, and recreational.

The administration of a temple is complex, involving management of vast properties and finances, and has evolved significantly over time, often leading to a power struggle between priestly and managerial authorities.

historical_figures.name: Heliodorus
historical_figures.significance: Erected a religious column in honour of Vāsudeva at Besnagar, providing one of the earliest inscriptional evidences of the Bhāgavata cult.

historical_figures.name: Gājāyana
historical_figures.significance: Constructed a stone-enclosure for the worship of Saṅkarṣaṇa and Vāsudeva at Ghosuṇḍi.

historical_figures.name: Khāravela
historical_figures.significance: Recorded to have repaired temples of different sects, suggesting the existence of temples in the first century.

historical_figures.significance: His work, Gāthā-saptaśatī, mentions the existence of temples.

historical_figures.name: Skanda-Mahāsena
historical_figures.significance: A temple dedicated to him is mentioned in the Bilsad inscription.

historical_figures.name: Kautilya
historical_figures.significance: His Artha-śāstra prescribes the building of temples for various deities, indicating state involvement in temple construction.

historical_figures.name: Appar, Sambandar and Sundara-mūrti
historical_figures.significance: Their compositions, known as 'tevāram' hymns, were taught in Śiva temples.

historical_figures.name: Āḻvārs
historical_figures.significance: Their compositions, known as 'prabhandam' hymnology, were taught in Vaiṣṇava shrines.

historical_figures.name: Varuṇa-śakti
historical_figures.significance: A renowned scholar who headed a major center of learning at the Kedāreśvara temple in Balligāme.

historical_figures.name: Keśava-deva
historical_figures.significance: Built a temple to Keśava in Balligāme and made provisions for thirty-eight scholars to reside there.

historical_figures.name: Śarvesvara-śakti-deva
historical_figures.significance: His maṭha is recorded to have had seventy-seven temples attached to it.

historical_figures.name: Tippu Sultan
historical_figures.significance: Initiated major changes in temple administration in 1788 by resuming temple lands and placing their management under state officials.

historical_figures.name: Kṛiṣṇarāja Odayar III
historical_figures.significance: Took personal interest in temple affairs and appointed local superintendents after the death of Tippu Sultan.

historical_figures.name: Sir Mark Cubbon
historical_figures.significance: As commissioner, he influenced the administration of temples in Mysore, at one point taking it out of the Commissioner's office.

historical_figures.name: Sir K. Sheshadri Iyer
historical_figures.significance: Found the administration of temples by Deputy Commissioners ineffective and appointed a separate Muzarai Superintendent.

controversial_points: The text notes a natural 'struggle to gain control over the temple and its properties' between the priests on one hand and the management on the other, highlighting an inherent tension in temple administration.

The historical account of temple administration in Mysore shows a progressive and ultimately complete takeover of temple management by the state government, a process that could be viewed as an erosion of the temple's traditional autonomy.
alternative_viewpoints: The chapter presents a largely cohesive, singular narrative of temple evolution and function. It does not explicitly engage with or present alternative scholarly viewpoints or debates on the origins of temples, the dating of Āgama texts, or the socio-economic impact of the temple system.
